newsitem.title: USA: ATHLETICS-O'BRIEN TO MISS WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS, CHALLENGES WINNER.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-O'BRIEN TO MISS WORLD CHAMPIONSHIPS, CHALLENGES WINNER.

text.p: Dan O'Brien regretfully announced Thursday he would miss next month's world athletics championships, but challenged the Athens decathlon winner to a duel at next year's Goodwill Games to determine the world's greatest athlete.
"I'm very disappointed to decline the invitation to the world championships," O'Brien said at a year-out news conference to promote next year's Goodwill Games in New York.
"I propose a challenge to whoever wins the decathlon in Athens to take me on next year at the Goodwill Games.
"I'm undefeated since '92 and until somebody beats me I still consider myself the world's greatest athlete."

O'Brien joined double Olympic champion Michael Johnson, Jackie Joyner-Kersee and figure skater Michelle Kwan to mark the year-out date of the Goodwill Games, which promise to draw a field of more than 1,300 athletes to a 15-sport competition offering $5 million in prize money and performance incentives.

Olympic champion and world record holder O'Brien pulled out of the U.S. nationals last month saying he had an apparent stress fracture in his right leg. The American said he was awaiting results of a bone scan on his left big toe and right leg but that he had to rule himself out of the worlds.
"It's a big disappointment. I would have liked to dominate all five world championships of the '90s," said O'Brien, who won the last three world championships in 1991, '93 and '95.
Two other prominent U.S. athletes have declared that they would miss the worlds.

U.S. 10,000 meters record holder Lynn Jennings, 37, said she would not run, citing "personal reasons." The six-time national champion owns a career best time of 31:19.89, which won her Olympic bronze at the Barcelona Games.
Sprinter Carlette Guidry also dropped off the U.S. team for Athens due to injury. Guidry, fourth in the 100 meters, was part of the pool for the 4x100 relay team.

O'Brien, who turns 31 Friday, said he believed he would have to learn to cope with his injury. "It's always there. It's a matter of pain tolerance," he said, before adding that he expected to achieve still more in sport.
"I still want to do some spectacular things before I retire in 2000 or 2001," he said.
O'Brien said he would resume serious training in mid-September. As for his immediate plans, he said: "I'm going to try to work on my golf game this summer. Try and hit it straighter."

Johnson, who pulled a leg muscle in his June 1 showdown sprint against Olympic 100 meters champion Donovan Bailey and has also complained recently of a back problem, said he was looking forward to Athens.
"Everything is fine as far as injuries," said Johnson, eager to avenge a loss three weeks ago in Paris that snapped his eight-year winning streak in the 400 meters.
Johnson said he was excited about getting the new wild card invitation to the world championships as a defending champion, despite having missed the U.S. nationals.
"The invitation to the world championships gives us the same attraction as the Goodwill Games already has," said Johnson. "The best athletes against the very best athletes.
